analysis.one_liner: Taxes US multinationals' profits from goods made abroad and imported back into the US.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: with no cosponsors and no committee action, it died in the Senate Finance Committee at the end of the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill changes the tax code so that when a US company's foreign subsidiary makes a product overseas and imports it back into the United States, that income counts as 'foreign base company income' and is taxed under the rules meant to capture offshore profits. It also applies the foreign tax credit limits separately to that income, and it would take effect for tax years after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and firms in domestic manufacturing, because the tax penalty makes it more expensive to move production overseas and import the goods back. The Treasury also gains revenue from closing part of the offshore-profit loophole.

how_it_helps.text: Adds 'imported property income' — profits from manufacturing, selling, or licensing property imported into the US by a controlled foreign corporation — to foreign base company income, so it is taxed under the anti-offshoring subpart F rules [S2][S3].

Captures income even when goods are sold to an unrelated importer who was expected to bring them into the US, closing a work-around, and applies foreign tax credit limits separately to this income so credits cannot shelter it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: US multinational corporations that produce goods abroad and import them into the United States, which would owe US tax on those profits that they currently do not.
analysis.who_pays_short: Multinationals that import goods made abroad

drawbacks.text: The tax would fall on profits from imported goods and could be passed to US consumers through higher prices, and compliance is complicated: the bill's own text carves out exceptions for re-exported property and agricultural commodities, showing how hard it is to draw the line [S3].

It taxes income at the subsidiary level through subpart F rules, which some economists argue can discourage foreign investment by US firms without bringing jobs home, and it applies only to imported goods, leaving services and other offshoring untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is straightforward: don't let US companies escape tax by making products overseas and selling them here. The main cost risks are higher import prices and compliance complexity, but the bill was never debated or amended, so no serious cost-benefit record exists.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2017 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on April 6, 2017; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee [S5].
No cosponsors ever joined the bill [S4].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 115th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US multinational corporations that manufacture abroad and import back into the US keep the current tax treatment of those profits, since the loophole was never closed.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no vote or party split ever emerged [S4][S5].

industries.industry: US multinational corporations with offshore manufacturing
industries.note: The bill would make their US tax bill on imported-property profits significantly higher, removing part of the tax advantage of making goods abroad and selling them in the US.
By taxing income from imported goods made by foreign subsidiaries, the bill would narrow the cost gap between offshore production and making goods in the United States.
